title: The Murle Homeland: Boma, Pibor and the Lands Between
subtitle: Understanding the land, rivers, highlands, lowlands and settlements that became central to Murle history and identity.
author: Murle Connect Editorial Team

body.heading: KOROK O MURLO
paragraphs: A people's history cannot be separated from the land in which that people lives. For the Murle, the homeland is not simply a territory drawn on a modern map. It is a landscape of mountains, plains, rivers, forests, grazing areas, farms, settlements and paths through which generations have lived and moved.

The Murle homeland is centred in the eastern part of South Sudan, particularly around the Pibor basin and the Boma highlands. Murle communities have also historically lived across the border in southwestern Ethiopia. The landscapes on both sides of the modern border are connected by older patterns of movement, family relationships, language and culture.

Boma and Pibor are especially important because they represent two major ecological environments within the wider Murle world. Boma is associated with highlands, hills and agricultural communities, while Pibor is dominated by broad lowlands, rivers, seasonal grasslands and a stronger pastoral and agro-pastoral way of life.
These differences have influenced how Murle communities live, but they do not divide them into separate peoples. Boma and Pibor are two important parts of the wider Murle homeland.

body.heading: Where Is the Murle Homeland?
paragraphs: The traditional Murle homeland lies in the eastern part of South Sudan, extending across the landscapes around the Pibor River and toward the Boma Plateau and the Ethiopian borderlands.

The area is geographically diverse. It includes highland areas around Boma, lower plains around Pibor, seasonal rivers, wooded areas, grasslands and wetlands. These environments support different forms of agriculture, livestock keeping, hunting and gathering.

Modern administrative boundaries do not completely describe the historical Murle homeland. The boundaries of present-day administrative areas were established long after Murle communities had developed their settlements and social institutions in the region.
For historical purposes, the Murle homeland is therefore better understood as a connected cultural landscape rather than only as an administrative unit.

body.heading: The Boma Highlands
paragraphs: The Boma highlands form one of the most important geographical areas in Murle history. The plateau and surrounding hills rise above the lower country and have their own climate, vegetation and agricultural conditions.

Murle communities living in the Boma area have traditionally relied heavily on cultivation. The highland environment provides opportunities for growing crops and maintaining settlements in places where the ecology differs significantly from the Pibor lowlands.

The hills and forests also provide resources such as wild foods, timber and areas for hunting. The landscape has therefore influenced not only the economy but also settlement patterns and everyday life.

Boma is also historically important because it became a major centre of Murle identity and community organization. Its importance is not limited to geography; it is part of the historical memory of the Murle people.

body.heading: The Pibor Lowlands
paragraphs: To the northwest of the Boma highlands lies the broader lowland environment associated with the Pibor River and its surrounding plains.

The Pibor basin has been particularly important to Murle pastoral and agro-pastoral life. Seasonal rainfall, rivers and floodplains provide water and grazing opportunities for livestock, while cultivated areas provide food crops.

The lowlands are not environmentally uniform. Conditions change with the seasons, and water and pasture are distributed differently throughout the year. This has encouraged patterns of movement between settlements, cattle camps, grazing areas and water sources.

For many lowland Murle communities, movement is therefore an organized part of life. Families and cattle may move according to environmental conditions while maintaining strong connections to particular home areas.

body.heading: The Pibor River
paragraphs: The Pibor River is one of the most important geographical features of the Murle lowlands. It is part of the wider river system that drains toward the Sobat and Nile systems.

For communities living around the river, water is essential for people, livestock and agriculture. The river and its surrounding environment also provide access to fishing, wild foods and other natural resources.
The Pibor River has therefore been much more than a physical feature. It has helped shape settlement, movement, economic life and the geography of communities.
The river also serves as an important reference point in understanding the wider Murle homeland. Many places and communities are connected directly or indirectly to the Pibor river system.

body.heading: The Lotilla and Veveno Rivers
paragraphs: The Pibor is part of a larger network of rivers and seasonal waterways. The Lotilla and Veveno are among the important waterways associated with the wider landscape in which Murle communities have lived.

These rivers and their tributaries provide water and create areas of pasture and cultivation. During the dry season, access to permanent or more reliable water sources becomes particularly important for people and livestock.

Seasonal flooding can also change the landscape. Areas that are dry at one time of the year may become flooded or greener during the rainy season. Murle livelihoods have developed in response to these seasonal changes.

The river systems therefore help explain why settlement and movement in Murle country have historically followed environmental patterns rather than remaining fixed in one location throughout the year.

body.heading: Kengen and the Eastern Landscape
paragraphs: The Kengen area forms part of the eastern landscape associated with Murle communities and their historical movements. Like other parts of the homeland, its importance is connected to water, pasture, settlement and relationships between communities.

The wider eastern Murle landscape also connects toward the Ethiopian border. This is significant because modern international boundaries divide areas that were historically connected through movement and interaction.

Families, livestock keepers, traders and other travellers have historically moved through broad areas rather than following today's political boundaries. The border between South Sudan and Ethiopia is therefore relatively recent when compared with the deeper history of the communities living in the region.

body.heading: Highlands and Lowlands
paragraphs: One of the most important geographical distinctions within Murle society is the difference between highland and lowland environments.

The Boma highlands have supported communities whose livelihoods have relied heavily on cultivation and settlement in the hills and plateau areas. The Pibor lowlands have supported communities whose livelihoods have relied more strongly on cattle keeping, seasonal movement, cultivation and the resources of the river plains.
These ecological differences have influenced food production, settlement patterns, livestock management and daily life. They have also contributed to different local experiences within Murle society.
Nevertheless, these differences do not mean that the highland and lowland Murle are separate ethnic groups. They share a broader language, ancestry, social relationships and cultural identity.

body.heading: Cattle and the Landscape
paragraphs: Cattle have played a central role in the history of many Murle communities, particularly in the lowlands. Livestock provide food and wealth and have important social and cultural functions.

Keeping cattle requires detailed knowledge of the environment. Herd owners need to know where water and pasture can be found during different seasons and how to move animals safely through the landscape.

Cattle camps can therefore be connected to wider systems of family, age-set and community organization. The movement of livestock also creates connections between different settlements and ecological zones.
In this way, cattle are not simply an economic resource. They are closely connected to Murle social life and to the relationship between people and their homeland.

body.heading: Agriculture in Murle Country
paragraphs: Agriculture has also been an important part of Murle life. Its importance varies according to environment, household circumstances and access to suitable land.

In the Boma highlands, cultivation has historically played a particularly important role because the environment provides conditions suitable for farming. Crops provide food and help support settled communities.

In the lowlands, cultivation exists alongside livestock keeping and is influenced strongly by rainfall, soil conditions and seasonal flooding. Households may combine farming with pastoral activities rather than depending entirely on one livelihood.
The combination of agriculture and livestock keeping has helped Murle communities adapt to an environment in which rainfall and water availability can change considerably between seasons.

body.heading: Seasonal Movement
paragraphs: Movement is one of the defining characteristics of life in the Murle lowlands. Seasonal movement allows people to respond to changes in rainfall, pasture and water availability.

This movement should not be confused with permanent migration. A family may have a recognized home area while also moving livestock to seasonal grazing areas. People can maintain strong social and cultural connections to a settlement even when part of the household is temporarily elsewhere.
Seasonal movement also requires cooperation. Knowledge about water, grazing, livestock health and safe routes is passed between generations and shared within communities.
This system developed because the environment itself changes throughout the year. Understanding Murle history therefore requires understanding the seasonal rhythm of the land.

body.heading: Settlements and Cattle Camps
paragraphs: Murle settlement patterns have traditionally reflected the different needs of farming, livestock keeping and access to water.

Permanent or semi-permanent settlements provide places where families can live, cultivate crops, maintain social relationships and participate in community life. Cattle camps serve different purposes and may be located closer to grazing and water resources.

The relationship between settlements and cattle camps creates a wider social network. Members of the same family or community may be distributed between different locations while remaining connected through kinship and shared responsibilities.

This pattern helps explain why the Murle homeland cannot be understood only by looking at permanent villages. The cultural landscape also includes seasonal camps, grazing areas, farms, rivers and routes of movement.

body.heading: The Homeland and Neighbouring Peoples
paragraphs: The Murle homeland has never existed in complete isolation from neighbouring communities. Dinka, Nuer, Anyuak, Toposa, Ethiopian communities and other peoples have lived in or around the wider eastern South Sudan region at different periods.
Relations between communities have changed over time. They have included trade, intermarriage, cultural exchange, alliances, competition over resources and periods of conflict.
Water and pasture can become especially important during periods of drought. When resources become scarce, competition can increase, while cooperation can also become necessary for survival.

Understanding these relationships requires listening to the histories of all communities involved. Murle history should not be written only as a story of conflict, just as the history of neighbouring peoples should not be reduced to conflict with the Murle.

body.heading: The Homeland before Modern Borders
paragraphs: The present-day border between South Sudan and Ethiopia is a modern political boundary. Murle communities and neighbouring peoples lived in the region long before this international border existed.
Historical movement was shaped more by rivers, mountains, grazing areas, settlements, kinship and political relationships than by international border posts.

This is particularly important for understanding Murle communities living near the Ethiopian border. People can share language and cultural connections even when they are citizens of different modern states.
The older cultural geography of the Murle therefore extends beyond the boundaries of the modern Republic of South Sudan.

body.heading: Boma and Pibor in Modern Administration
paragraphs: Modern government has introduced administrative boundaries and institutions into the Murle homeland. Pibor became an important administrative centre during the twentieth century and later became the centre of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area.
The Greater Pibor Administrative Area is a modern political and administrative structure. It should not be confused with the much older historical Murle homeland.

The creation of modern administrative structures changed the way government services, security, education and political representation were organized. At the same time, customary institutions and local community relationships continued to influence everyday life.
The modern administrative map is therefore another layer placed over a much older cultural landscape.

body.heading: The Homeland as Cultural Memory
paragraphs: For the Murle, places carry memories. A river can be connected to an ancestral story. A hill can be associated with settlement. A grazing area can be remembered through generations of cattle camps. A village can become connected to important families and events.

This relationship between people and place is one reason why geography is so important to Murle history. The homeland is not simply where people happen to live. It is part of how historical memory is organized.

When elders describe the movements of earlier generations, they often connect those movements to recognizable landscapes. Place names therefore become important historical sources and deserve careful documentation.
Preserving Murle place names and the stories associated with them can help future generations understand the relationship between their people and their homeland.

body.heading: A Homeland under Pressure
paragraphs: The Murle homeland has experienced major changes during the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Civil wars, displacement, insecurity, environmental pressure, population movement and changing political boundaries have all affected communities.
Climate variability also places pressure on pastoral and agricultural livelihoods. Changes in rainfall and water availability can affect pasture, crops, livestock and the timing of seasonal movement.
Modern infrastructure and growing towns are changing the landscape as well. Roads, schools, health facilities, markets and administrative centres create new patterns of movement and settlement.
These changes do not mean that traditional relationships with the land have disappeared. Instead, Murle communities are continually adapting old knowledge to new circumstances.

body.heading: Why Boma and Pibor Matter
paragraphs: Boma and Pibor matter to Murle history because they represent two major centres of a wider homeland.
Boma represents the highlands, hills, forests and agricultural communities. Pibor represents the river plains, cattle camps, seasonal movement and agro-pastoral life of the lowlands.
Together, these environments demonstrate the ability of Murle society to adapt to very different ecological conditions while maintaining a common identity.
The relationship between Boma and Pibor is therefore not a story of two separate peoples. It is a story of one people living across different landscapes.

body.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The Murle homeland is a landscape shaped by water, mountains, rivers, grasslands, farms, cattle camps and settlements. Its history cannot be separated from the people who have lived and moved across it for generations.

The Boma highlands and Pibor lowlands are particularly important centres of Murle life. Their environments are different, and those differences have produced different patterns of farming, livestock keeping and settlement.

The Pibor, Lotilla, Veveno and Kengen river systems form part of a wider landscape that has supported communities through changing seasons. The Boma hills and plateau provide another environment in which Murle communities have built homes, farms and social institutions.
Modern administrative boundaries have added new political divisions to this older cultural landscape, but they have not erased the deeper connections between Murle communities.

To understand the Murle people is therefore also to understand their homeland. The land is not merely the setting of Murle history. It is one of the forces that shaped the people's movement, livelihoods, relationships and identity.
Boma and Pibor are different landscapes, but together they remain central to the story of the Murle people.

historicalNote: This article describes the Murle homeland using geographical, anthropological and historical perspectives. References to Boma, Pibor, seasonal movement, pastoralism, agriculture and neighbouring communities describe broad historical patterns and may vary between local communities and periods. Modern administrative boundaries should not be confused with the older cultural geography of Murle communities.
